>We should begin by leveraging sdbusplus::async infrastructure for our current needs.

I’m unclear on how we’re expected to use libspdm in a non-blocking way without modifying it directly. My specific concern is around how all libspdm calls can be integrated into an asynchronous or concurrent flow.

I had a discussion with Steven yesterday, and he confirmed that there is currently no ongoing effort to make the libspdm API asynchronous. He also mentioned that making the API async would involve a significant amount of work.

As a potential solution, I propose using a multi-threaded model, where each thread maintains its own spdm_context and independently handles a request. However, I haven’t come across any OpenBMC user-space applications that follow this multithreaded approach with libspdm. I have not protyped this approach, If we all are aligned, I can prototype this.

Proposed Options

Option 1: Use libspdm as-is and serialize all SPDM requests

All requests are processed one at a time.

Limitation: If the system has 10 devices, a user cannot retrieve attestation data from a device while another request is in progress.

Option 2: Use a multi-threaded model

Each request is handled by a dedicated worker thread, each with its own spdm_context.

This allows concurrent handling of requests, avoiding the bottleneck of serialization.

Option 3: Modify libspdm to support async APIs

Requires changes to the libspdm internals to support asynchronous operation.

This would provide more flexibility but involves a significant development effort.

Question

What approach should we proceed with?

I’m leaning towards Option 2 (multithreaded model) as a balanced approach, offering concurrency without requiring deep changes to libspdm.
We can go with option 1 too now for the simplicity - and start working for option3 later.

I think an easier approach is:

option2a: all spdm blocking calls are delegated to a single extra thread and the delegation-completion is signaled via a co_await. 

I can help with “how” to do this if needed but it sets everything up in a way that it is mostly a trivial change over to option 3 when ready. The important thing to me is that dbus responses by the daemon are non-blocking so that services like object-mapper can always interrogate the spdm daemon.

Thanks, Patrick for the suggeation, I will reach out if I need help to implement this.

I do have one more question: even with this approach, we’re still effectively handling one request at a time — meaning the coroutine remains blocked until the thread finishes the SPDM blocking call.

I was concerned about the performance impact. Our system has over 25 devices, and we need to retrieve attestation data from each of them approximately once per minute. With a single-threaded delegation model, this could become a bottleneck.

Would you see any issues with creating a dedicated thread per device, so each device can be handled independently? This might help us achieve better concurrency and meet our timing requirements.

> I do have one more question: even with this approach, we’re still effectively handling one request at a time — meaning the coroutine remains blocked until the thread finishes the SPDM blocking call.

The co-routine that initiated the "request to do some SPDM stuff" is blocked, yes, but it is blocked until you do the SPDM work anyhow.

> I was concerned about the performance impact. Our system has over 25 devices, and we need to retrieve attestation data from each of them approximately once per minute.

Are these 25 devices all on different busses?  If not, aren't you going to block anyhow?

> Would you see any issues with creating a dedicated thread per device, so each device can be handled independently? This might help us achieve better concurrency and meet our timing requirements.

I'd rather see a straight-forward implementation and get measurements first.  Depending on what bus we're talking about, 25 devices once per minute still shouldn't be an issue.  A single 400kbps I2C bus can probably still get that done.

(Having a "requirement" to re-gather the attestation information every minute off 25 sub-devices seems a bit strange to me though.)

Rather than a "dedicated thread per device", I think it would be way simpler to have a threadpool (which you could compile-time set to 25 if you needed on your system).  You need a workqueue of sorts anyhow in order to get the co-routine to block, dispatch the work to a SPDM worker, etc.  So, having this queue be acted on by multiple threads probably isn't a large lift.

At some point we do have to question how much work this is to do multi-threaded vs just doing the necessary in libspdm to make it async.

>Are these 25 devices all on different busses? If not, aren't you going to block anyhow?
No, It is on the same bus, but in MCTP it is not a blocking implementation, They semd the packet asynchronously to multiple endpoints.

>Rather than a "dedicated thread per device", I think it would be way simpler to have a threadpool (which you could compile-time set to 25 if you needed on your system). You need a workqueue of sorts anyhow in order to get the co-routine to block, dispatch the work to a SPDM worker, etc. So, having this queue be acted on by multiple threads probably isn't a large lift.

I am implementing both approaches to do the performance test.

Implementation 1 :
Uses pure coroutine/co_await pattern
Direct integration with SPDM calls
No explicit thread management
Uses std::async with proper coroutine suspension/resumption

Implementation 2 :
Had threads inside coroutines
Used explicit thread management with std::unique_ptr<std::thread>
More complex resource management

I plan to create two prototype commits that will allow us to:
Compare the performance and behavior of both approaches.

I have tested both implementations on VCA with three devices so far. I now plan to extend the testing to include Certificate and Measurement support, along with a few additional devices.

However, I will be pushing both prototype commits so that you can review them and get the feedback early on the issues.
